issue.title: Different timezone in Ubuntu leads to data.AuthorDate being NA in parse_gitlog()

labels.name: type:bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issue.body:
Bug found by @massihonda 

Quoting e-mail exchange:

# Problem

> In the script gitlog_showcases.Rmd, the function parse_gitlog should create a dataframe with a column that records the date of the commits (data.AuthorDate). However, in my environment this column is filled with NA. So, in the part project_git_slice it does not select any raw, because none of them have a date.

# Workaround

>  After inserting the line Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "C"), the timestamps were correctly assessed and the scripts ran properly. 

# Root Cause

> The problem was in the function as.POSIXct, because I think the date format in my laptop did not match (my date is by default in italian format). The command Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "C") changes the format in my laptop to the english format. (source: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45565986/as-posixlt-returns-na).. The parameter "C" is OS dependent, in Windows I think it is "English".

milestone.title: 0.0.0.9000 Recreate Smells Study Analysis
milestone.description: The existing analysis is no longer runnable. See #17 for details.

issue.body:
The purpose of this issue is to understand how can a dev-file network can be obtained at function granularity. The following links are cues to that. A more organized analysis is done in further comments. 

This file from Codeface employs ctags:

https://github.com/siemens/codeface/blob/e6640c931f76e82719982318a5cd6facf1f3df48/codeface/cluster/cluster.py#L1414

Exuberant Ctags basically is a parser that takes as input a source file (e.g. bla.py) and outputs metadata of functions and other data objects of said source code as another file. Making sense of the metadata file appears to be very confusing, see this question on SO:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41933837/understanding-the-ctags-file-format

However, Codeface relies on a python library to parse Ctags, making it much simpler. This implementation appears to be very efficient, as it seems to be just a wrapper to a C file that does the parsing (notice the github project hasn't be updated in a long while):

https://github.com/cloggo/python-ctags

Codeface also relies on this VCS python package, which appears to abstract implementations of version control systems (Git, Subversion):

https://github.com/codeinn/vcs

Lastly, I also found out Exuberant Ctags itself has been abandoned, and other project took over forking it since then: 

https://ctags.io/

issue.title: Improve file filters with Humberto suggestions

labels.name: type:enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

issue.body:
Current file filter allows for the config file to specify for a given project:

- Include only specified file extensions
- Filter any files with the word `test` on it. 

Additional files and example use cases that can be implemented are as follows:

> Projects analyses should not include test files
> - Exclude files that have “test” on the package
> - Exclude files that have “example”, or “sample” in the path
> - Exclude generated source code

> And they also exclude anything that is not source code.  In their case that is .java files.  In our case we can enumerate the languages. It's not a large set (e.g. .java, .cc, .c, .h, etc.) and exclude other files.

> **Generated source code**: Some frameworks, for example "Mapstruct" (https://mapstruct.org/) generate implementation code from interfaces. This is the kind of code we are talking about, since it is not written by the developers.

> Project with "example" files:
> https://github.com/apache/calcite
> https://github.com/apache/pdfbox

> Project with "tutorial" files:
> https://github.com/apache/ant

> We consider that these are not "core" files of the project and this is why we decided to ignore them.

issue.body:
While this may seem like a reverse from #33, I have observed git log interfaces allow for grep filtering the commit messages ([and even the source code down the road if we so decide](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/22055390/how-to-install-git-with-pcre-support-on-osx-with-homebrew)), while perceval interface will not afford me the luxury.

This functionality is very important for the analysis of massive project git logs like Chromium, which have 20GB of data when our interest is on very specific commits. The filtering from raw is much faster, and most importantly, avoid choking R by trying to pass a 20GB blob on memory to then parse the data. 
 
If we want to only get the git log containing certain bug ids from Chromium, we can have git log do that for us like so: 

`git log --no-merges master --grep="(?i)bug=119250|bug=117627" --perl-regexp`

This specifies we do not want merge commits, that we want to look only on the master branch, and the regular expression to apply. `(?i)` [will make the word bug case insensitive to match](https://regular-expressions.mobi/modifiers.html?wlr=1). 

Using the option `--perl-regexp` is important, otherwise, git log will not understand `|` as OR operator. The example above applied to chromium returned nothing without using it. When using `--perl-regexp` one problem I encountered was the following error on OS X Catalina 10.15.1:

```
cannot use Perl-compatible regexes when not compiled with USE_LIBPCRE
```

The following stackoverflow suggested [upgrading via brew](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/22055390/how-to-install-git-with-pcre-support-on-osx-with-homebrew). I noticed my installation was from elsewhere under version `git version 2.23.0`. 

Brew installation as of this date is `git 2.27.0`. Simply installing the current brew git, and accepting it's suggestion to overwrite the existing git symlinks:

```
==> Installing git
==> Pouring git-2.27.0.catalina.bottle.tar.gz
Error: The `brew link` step did not complete successfully
The formula built, but is not symlinked into /usr/local
Could not symlink bin/git
Target /usr/local/bin/git
already exists. You may want to remove it:
  rm '/usr/local/bin/git'

To force the link and overwrite all conflicting files:
  brew link --overwrite git

To list all files that would be deleted:
  brew link --overwrite --dry-run git
```

Sufficed to enable the --perl-regexp. 

With these changes in place, and git enabled to use compatible regular expressions, Kaiaulu can them leverage this new interface to sub-set Chromium's 20GB log into very few megabytes, and use Perceval or any other git log parser to parse as json the much smaller dataset.

issue.title: MPL 2.0 License and necessary codebase changes

labels.name: type:refactoring
labels.description: Code changes that improve maintenability, performance, etc

labels.name: type:milestone
labels.description: Issues representing milestones since they don't recognize markdown...

issue.body:
Both me and @rnkazman are in agreement to go with a MPL 2.0 instead of GPL, for the reasons stated [here](https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/pull/2456). 

As of this version, however, my guess is that the code can't "legally" be redistributed due to any potential conflict of licenses themselves OR otherwise is implicitly GPL. This issue contains collected links, evidence, or sanity checking on the best course to go about this, and to index needed changes in order to go with the said license. This whole issue is of course IANAL. 

# 1. R is GPL, does that make anything R GPL? 

Maybe. 

1.1 Not because of the R language per se, according to this [twitter discussion](https://twitter.com/hadleywickham/status/821762007980527618) between Hadley and another person, which cites, in turn, [this page from the GPL license](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.en.html#IfInterpreterIsGPL):

> When the interpreter just interprets a language, the answer is no. The interpreted program, to the interpreter, is just data; a free software license like the GPL, based on copyright law, cannot limit what data you use the interpreter on. You can run it on any data (interpreted program), any way you like, and there are no requirements about licensing that data to anyone.

> However, when the interpreter is extended to provide “bindings” to other facilities (often, but not necessarily, libraries), the interpreted program is effectively linked to the facilities it uses through these bindings. 

However, maybe yes because all functions from `base R` are themselves license as GPL, a point raised on the discussion: 

> That clause is very explicit re library bindings — in this case, all of base R, which is GPL. 

There is a [public statement from R foundation that seems to discourage this interpretation](https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/2009-May/053248.html), but it's murky. The same argument is also [raised here](https://www.reddit.com/r/Rlanguage/comments/axixsd/r_packages_for_commercial_purposes/) concerning using base R. 

More on the confusion is summarized in this [Reddit thread](https://old.reddit.com/r/Rlanguage/comments/63ha4q/gpl_license_and_r_programs/) which someone even suggests the NAMESPACE forces GPL too:

> IANAL, but I think as soon as you build a package that imports function from other packages using the NAMESPACE mechanism of R that use gpl your package also needs to be distributed with gpl. This has to do with linking. As described in the same faq.

In short: It is not clear if using Base R or simply using the R package mechanism implies GPL. I believe `data.table`, [an R package who recently switched from GPL to MPL 2.0](https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/pull/2456) gets away with this because they do not use base R themselves. 

Apparently, we don't use it either for now, but it's hard to say if we won't in the future. 

# 2. Dynamically Linking with GPL packages. 

## 2.1 `library(aGPLlibrary)`

The second and more prominent problem comes from this. Specifically, using `library(aGPLlibrary)` seems to falls under the clause from GPL that the entire codebase must turn GPL. [According to GNU website](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#GPLPlugins):

> It depends on how the main program invokes its plug-ins. If the main program uses fork and exec to invoke plug-ins, and they establish intimate communication by sharing complex data structures, or shipping complex data structures back and forth, that can make them one single combined program. A main program that uses simple fork and exec to invoke plug-ins and does not establish intimate communication between them results in the plug-ins being a separate program.

> If the main program dynamically links plug-ins, and they make function calls to each other and share data structures, we believe they form a single combined program, which must be treated as an extension of both the main program and the plug-ins. If the main program dynamically links plug-ins, but the communication between them is limited to invoking the ‘main’ function of the plug-in with some options and waiting for it to return, that is a borderline case.

The interpretation above has been associated to give a margin of doubt on `library(aGPLlibrary)` being viral, and is why data.table turned MPL 2.0. 

In short, for our purposes, this means we have to let go of 4 of the current packages currently in use to avert trouble: 

 * stringr (>= 1.4.0),
 * jsonlite (>= 1.6),
 * igraph (>= 1.2.5)
 * lubridate 

I am not sure yet if this is possible for `stringr` (the other option would be baseR), and for `jsonlite` (not sure on an option yet). `lubridate` alternative may also be just baseR. 

`igraph` can possibly be circumvented, save for the projection operation to generate co-change, and thus file-file network projections weighted by number of modifications). Then again, DV8 provides HDSMs, which could be parsed to construct a file-file network weighted by number of modifications.

The second change is that the parse_igraph functions would be modified to not output igraph objects (as I can't load the library). Rather, it would output edgelists with type and weight, a common public format widely adopted to represent graphs, much like adjacent matrices and not particular to `igraph`. This in turn could be used by a GPL igraph notebook in a separate repo to showcase the work. 

The good news is that the visualization library itself I use is MIT licensed: https://github.com/datastorm-open/visNetwork/blob/master/DESCRIPTION so maybe even the visualizations can be made available still, without relying on igraph. 

## 2.2 Can we refer to any GPL code at all?

This was the next  pertinent question: Currently Kaiaulu relies on data output by a GPL program, namely `Perceval`. Perceval parses the gitlog for us, so we don't need to reinvent the wheel. Is that a problem? Well, again the answer depends, but this time it seems favorable to us. 

Specifically, Kaiulu interacts with Perceval (and to many more tools in the future) via command line. For example:

https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/77f0d667aba9a316734407d70c58152b8e5a2958/R/parsers.R#L27-L31

What does GPL says about this? GPL says [maybe again](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#MereAggregation). However, the general intuition I draw from it is that it is ok if your code does not look like a wrapper to the program itself. I am emphasizing the items by separating in bullets below, but the original text contains none:

 1. **Where's the line between two separate programs, and one program with two parts?** This is a legal question, which ultimately judges will decide. We believe that a proper criterion depends both on the mechanism of communication (exec, pipes, rpc, function calls within a shared address space, etc.) and the semantics of the communication (what kinds of information are interchanged).
 2. If the modules are included in the same executable file, they are definitely combined in one program. 
 3. If modules are designed to run linked together in a shared address space, that almost surely means combining them into one program.
 4. **By contrast, pipes, sockets and command-line arguments are communication mechanisms normally used between two separate programs. So when they are used for communication, the modules normally are separate programs.**
    4.1 **But if the semantics of the communication are intimate enough, exchanging complex internal data structures, that too could be a basis to consider the two parts as combined into a larger program.**

In essence, we fall under item 4, and I believe items 1 to 3 are the reason why Section 2.2 of this issue is so confusing. 

Does our use of Perceval fall under 4.1? I doubt it. We just get the data it downloads from elsewhere parsed. Moreover, I think my reasoning on going forward with [OO-R6](https://github.com/r-lib/R6), which is also a package under MIT license, also seems to make sense [due to the following discussion](https://github.com/dselivanov/text2vec/issues/109#issuecomment-231979071):

> I have checked a legal books about GPL (unfortunately it s in French: Droit des logiciels - édition Puf - F Pellegrini et S. Canevet) and basically, to avoid contamination of a project with GPL2 licence, you need to wrap the GPL2 code and access to it through a generic interface.

>  **This interface should make it possible to use code from other projects with similar functionalities than the GPL code. One interesting point is that to make it work, another project with similar function but under another licence should exist.**

> **The implementation of the other project has not to be written, but just be easily possible. The idea is that it should be easy to replace the code under GPL with another one because of the interface (like a lego block).**

> The approach is inspired of how to limit GPL2 contamination because of the Linux kernel executing some non GPL code.

> In general, my opinion is to limit the consequences of GPL code to the final user.
For instance, forcing the user to install another package to get some functions just for legal reasons is really an overkill. And letting the GPL licence contamining the whole project and making it impossible to use for some startup seems not Ok at all.

This means #11 is ideal. Having abstract classes defining how other interfaces can integrate clearly goes along with the description above:

 * Perceval is not the only git log parser. 
 * igraph is not the only program who processes edgelists 

Etc.



# 3. Another use case and a few more examples: Xgboost 

This library was also [subject to the same concerns](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/issues/1338). The discussion covers a lot of points not covered here. But, being a prominent library we can piggyback on some practices. Namely:

 * An alternative to `stringr` is [`stringi`](https://github.com/gagolews/stringi), which is not GPL, as xgboost did. 
 * igraph is `ok` to be added under `Suggested` packages, and even code can be made available to plot, provided an alternative interface is available. See [here](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/blob/84a3af8dc00dbc587d55892a55b418d362e24ff5/R-package/R/xgb.plot.deepness.R#L70-L71) for an example where igraph code is available as an **alternative**. 
 * The package `DESCRIPTION`(https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/blob/646def51e02d4017ac85065a10ca763e8941d62a/R-package/DESCRIPTION) file has a good guideline overall to where GPL packages and other permissive licenses packages should be. 
 * It also shows I should move the packages from Depends to Import as a good practice, to enforce explicit call of the functions with package names, as I am already doing anyway. 
 * [This](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/pull/1401) is a fantastic PR with several commits showing how to reduce GPL dependency and risk of infection. In particular [the commit switching from stringr to stringi](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/pull/1401/commits/de4b3b9877f8ac9d985edcdf27ad97cc2187c25e), and the commit creating a generic interface to [ggplot](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/pull/1401/commits/331a196535313aca07a660568d64e75e835813aa). 
   * Finally note the way to provide a generic interface is to use **base R** as the default. Which clears our concern that base R should be OK to use, all else failing. 
  * Writing Vignettes with igraph should be OK too! This [example](https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost/blob/646def51e02d4017ac85065a10ca763e8941d62a/R-package/vignettes/xgboostfromJSON.Rmd) which uses the jsonlite, a GPL library I must replace, is included in the vignette. From the R package standpoint that is considered OK, because the vignette is to showcase problems of someone having data originally in JSON. XGboost itself does not require json data, but a .csv file. Hence, it is OK to use. For our purposes, making the case we don't need a json library could be possible, but this would be very inconvenient. 

# 4. Remaining Challenges 

Finding a json library that is not GPL based, and any package that helps with replacing lubridate should be it. For lubridate maybe `?IDateTime` will do, which is from data.table, albeit experimental.

Edit: Disregard jsonlite concern. [It is MIT licensed](https://github.com/jeroen/jsonlite/blob/master/DESCRIPTION). I don't know where I got the idea it wasn't.

Edit 2: See also: https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2008-July/169332.html

Edit 3: See this to handle dates without lubridate: http://biostat.mc.vanderbilt.edu/wiki/pub/Main/ColeBeck/datestimes.pdf
